So the entire lengthy column together with the journalists set out and at the first barricades we found our MP whom I know and he told me that I should be the one who would say who could come to Bijeljina with us. I set up the column. Of course the general that was with us, he was the first that I appointed to come with us, the troops that were escorting him, and then of course Mr. Fikret Abdic together with his escorts. "Reporter Vukasinovic: How come that they went to the barracks first? "Biljana Plavsic: I wanted to come here first -- "Reporter Vukasinovic: What kind of a conflict was there? "Biljana Plavsic: Well, I wanted to come here first. I wanted to contact the Crisis Staff, first me, and then I wanted to talk to them. I will go to the barracks as well. "Reporter Vukasinovic: Do you perhaps know what was going on in the barracks, why did they want to go there first? "Biljana Plavsic: No, I have no idea. "Reporter Vukasinovic: I mean, there are soldiers in the barracks. I don't know. "Biljana Plavsic: Well, here's why. I mean, let me tell you, this is without any -- don't think there is any evil intent here. We were escorted by the police from Bijeljina. I mean from Tuzla. A military patrol escorted us to Tuzla. We arrived all the way up to Tuzla. So perhaps I should have gone to the barracks first, but since I am my own boss, it was my choice to first visit the local Serbian people's Crisis Staff and meet here with Mr. Arkan and his associates here. We are fortunate to have met here even Mr. Goran Adzic [sic] and so on. I knew that it would be better to have such a close encounter without the others and that we will talk later with everybody. "Reporter Vukasinovic: Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, my question to you is this: Based on what we have just seen -- let me first ask you this: Are you aware of this event, of this visit by Mrs. Biljana Plavsic to the Crisis Staff, or rather, to Arkan, and Goran Hadzic was also present there. Are you aware of that event?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. I saw that on TV Nis, and then Biljana Plavsic told me and bragged that Arkan was the first Serbian general that she had ever kissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that Arkan had either arrived in Bijeljina at Mrs. Plavsic's request or at least with her blessing? Based on what she told you and based on what we have just seen in the courtroom, would you agree with such a proposition?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that she came across Arkan in Bijeljina and that later on she agreed to his stay there, since she kissed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to tender that footage into evidence now, please, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Admitted as Exhibit D00052. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D52 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness look at 65 ter document 2D115 next, please. May we turn to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, is this your document, although it's not signed, but I assume that you'll recognise it. Is it your document dated the 31st of March, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And unless I'm very much mistaken, it is your order for the so-called spring offensive in the spring of 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now display page 2 for the witness, please. Paragraph 2. I apologise, but may we have the top of the page displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The paragraph beginning with "In the meantime ..." General --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might just inquire. I'm not sure whether --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not sure if there's a problem with our e-court system, but I'm unable to find a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is that there seems to be no translation in e-court from what I can see, the original being in B/C/S. By the way, this seems not to be the real original, is it, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to apologise and tell you, or rather, apologise because we don't have the translation on e-court. So I'd like to apologise for that. We've only just found it recently. That's the first point. And secondly, it was submitted for translation. Now, this is a copy of the document, but perhaps it would be best to ask the witness whether it is the document that he signed and when he signed it and whether it is an authentic document because I don't know anything about it. It was found in the database that the Prosecution disclosed to us. So I think that it would be best to ask the General with respect to the authenticity of the document and what kind of document it is. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you asked the witness whether he thought this was an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, may we have your comments, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document has no signature. The contents and the time it was issued confirm that it is my document or tells me that it is my document. However, I've already seen this document somewhere because I can see that my initials are up there next to your number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are your initials at the top of the page, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there's a date with it at the beginning of the document, the 8th of July, 2009. Do you have -- in apparently the same colour of handwriting. Is that your handwriting? Do you recognise on the first page the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is my handwriting, and I know with which investigator I did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this to say that you had a conversation in July 2009 with an investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was a statement taken then or an -- who was the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that Nicholas was the lawyer, but I don't know the name of the investigator, a tall, thin man. They didn't take any statement. All they asked me was to see if I recognised some documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're talking about an investigator, did you -- to what party, if any, that investigator was related, Prosecution or local authorities? Do you have any recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean who the accused was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- yes -- well, whatever. You are talking about an investigator. I've got no knowledge about investigator of what party, to what proceedings. Was it the Prosecution? Was it the Defence team? The Defence team of what accused? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person representing the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you remember in -- the Prosecution related to what case before this Tribunal? Was it for this case or was it for another case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't linked to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If it assists the Chamber, Mr. Laugel has located an English translation. He's in the process of uploading it. Perhaps if Mr. Petrovic withdraws his request to have the document translated, we should have this document up shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then -- could it then be made available for Mr. Petrovic to be attached to his uploaded document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, my question -- well, can we have page 2 displayed again, please, on our screens. My question to you is this: Is it true and correct that in the Posavina region forces did appear which were denoted as being Arkan's and that those forces were under the protection of MUP of Republika Srpska during this time too, that is to say in the spring of 1994? Is that the piece of information that you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I have a problem with this document. I saw a moment ago in the upper right-hand corner underneath your number it says "copy." And there's -- and my signature is not there at the bottom. Now, what you asked me, whether I knew that these groups moved around, yes, I did have knowledge of that. And usually they were passing through between Bijeljina, Banja Luka, and the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is what it says here correct, that those groups were under the protection of the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how this information came to be in your document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably received from the command of the Eastern Bosnia or 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence as well, please. And we shall be providing the translation -- or rather, can it be MFI'd? And once we receive the translation, I'd like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I reserve my position until I see the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not for MFI?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not for MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the MFI number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D00053, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D53 keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a document here which might help us to throw more light on the authenticity of the previous document, and that is document 2D116. So may we have that document called up, and I do believe that we have a translation of it. Do we? No, we don't. I apologise. We don't. But I think that the witness might be assisted by looking at 2D216 [as interpreted], and with your permission, Your Honours, I will read the central paragraph, which is a brief one, of this document, so that you can understand what it's about and follow. And there's a correction to the text of the directive on the 31st of March, 1994. Looking into the main document and the encoded text, confidential 02-2, et cetera, a mistake was made which was made in the encoding. The text of the passage from the order should read as follows: In the meantime, in the area of Serbian Posavina, paramilitary organisations have appeared, Arkan's men, NOs, and others, who unfortunately with the MUP's acquiescence of the Republic of Serbia are running around Posavina and advocating some kind of -- so MUP of Republika Srpska -- MUP of Republika Srpska, not the Republic of Serbia. Republika Srpska, running around Posavina advocating some kind of re-integration of the former Yugoslavia. They're doing everything in their power for the Muslim/Croatian forces to cut the corridor, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, this is a document which was sent by teleprinter, but you're the signatory. Now, can we agree that this is one of your documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to express my concern that what's now recorded in the transcript is -- appears to be in quotations -- a quote from the document, when, in fact, it's a mixture of a quote from the document and a quote from Mr. Petrovic. I just want to note that fact. I guess perhaps we'll have to wait until we have the actual translation to clarify what the document actually says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have no idea whether it's a mixture or not, but I do agree with you that we should have a look at the official translation before we even can find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave I totally agree with my learned friend. There has been a mistake in the transcript and I intervened, and then that has been corrected. But there was a mix-up in the meantime. However, I would like to limit myself to the issue of the authenticity of the document. I would like to hear from the document -- the witness whether this was a document drafted by him or not. And for the rest of the issues relating to this document, I would like to reserve the right to discuss those when we have the translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is on the record now. Please proceed and ask the witness what you want to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document please be MFI'd and could it please be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit once we are able to provide a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document can be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And again I'd reserve my position until I can read the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked for identification as D00054. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Mr. Petrovic, now apparently there has been a document dated 31st of March and then we have another document which says it's not accurate, it should read differently. Now, I have not compared the two, but is now the document you'd shown first, is that the one which is already corrected or is that the one still to be corrected?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the second, shorter document is the correction of the first document, dated the 31st of March, and only one part of one paragraph, the paragraph that I asked the witness about and the paragraph that the witness testified about. So the first document has been corrected by the second document, and that's the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the correction is already included in the document as you had shown it to us earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, I don't think so. The first document has remained what it was, and a correction has been made in one paragraph. And this was done to provide the addressee with a complete information, because the way I understood it there was -- a mistake was made during the decoding. But maybe the General would be best suited to actually tell us what happened with that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Milovanovic, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first document it says that the paramilitary units were running around Republika Srpska under the protection of the Ministry of the Interior, and that was then corrected. And the correction refers to the part "under the protection." So the words "under the protection" has been replaced by the words "with the blessing of" or "in full knowledge of."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which was translated to us as "with the acquiescence," I think. It's clear -- the correction is not yet -- so therefore the first document is authentic to the extent that it was the first version, but is not authentic as not being the final version of what this document was supposed to be. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock. Perhaps I should say please do not proceed at this moment. I would like to know, Mr. Petrovic, where we are in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sure that we will finish with this witness by the end of the day. I believe that I need another half an hour to 45 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- I can see that you would be happy to finish the witness today, but there may be questions in re-examination. Mr. Groome, how much time do you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would estimate that I would have ten minutes of questions. And then it would -- may I expedite things. I'm going to ask that the witness be allowed to read a document rather than read it in front of us. I'll show it -- with the Court's permission, I'll show it to counsel and then perhaps we could bring it in -- the Court Usher could bring it in to the witness during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then, of course, we do not know whether there would be -- whether the re-examination triggers any need for further cross. Let me check with my colleagues as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, in view of the time that remains, we'll have a break until five minutes to 6.00, perhaps I should add sharp; and then you have 40 minutes, not more, Mr. Petrovic, to conclude your cross-examination. And then we'll finish the testimony of this witness by 7.00, at its latest. We have a -- we resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, I have just a few more questions, so I hope we'll end this foray into the documents. Now, I'd like to ask you to look at D29.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have it up on e-court, please. It's a very short document. D29 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at that document, please, General. Can I ask you the question now?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This letter, this is Arkan's letter to Radovan Karadzic in actual fact. Now, my question to you is: Did the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska know about the existence of certain special relations with Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, at the material time, the time we're talking about, did you have any awareness of that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now look at P289, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2 of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It is signed by General, or rather, Ratko Mladic's signature is there, Colonel-General Ratko Mladic. Would you look at the paragraph that begins with Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, is showing citizens an official document, et cetera, that document.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean to myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, read it to yourself so that you can acquaint yourself with the contents of the document. And now let's look at the second page under number 1 where it says: "I demand and propose ..." Read that section, please, and see what General Mladic is proposing.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this document it says that Colonel-General Ratko Mladic is asking the president of Republika Srpska to take away the authorisation to Zeljko Raznatovic, authorising him to arrest -- use his troops to arrest people, et cetera. Now, knowing General Mladic and knowing the information that he had, would General Mladic have ever comprised a document of this kind had he not had reliable information that this kind of authorisation existed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic and I worked on problems of this nature together. He asked Karadzic to withdraw the authorisation, and I asked Karadzic to organise a meeting with me and Arkan. We were not sure whether those authorisations existed, but Arkan did present some papers and documents which he said was the authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now play a brief film, an excerpt, which I'd like you to view, General. It is P59. And as we were explained, it's a film that was taken on the 10th of November, 1995. And I'd like it played from the first minute until the fourth minute of the tape. Let's view that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Unknown Soldier: Sir, the battalion of the Serbian Volunteer Guard is lined up in your honour, sir. Ranks are ready for inspection. "Radovan Karadzic: For the guard and for you as the commander of the guard. "Zeljko Raznatovic: Thank you very much, Mr. President. "Radovan Karadzic: Gratitude for you being here. This is not the end, it is the beginning. "Zeljko Raznatovic: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Would you be so kind as to say a few words. "Radovan Karadzic: I am deeply thankful and I congratulate you and I hope that we will meet again in peace. And you will always have a place in the heart of those whom you have defended. Thank you. "Zeljko Raznatovic: Mr. President, in the name of the Serbian Volunteer Guards I would like to say two words to you, which is that we are ready if you call us and that we will be back to defend our eternal homeland, to defend our women and children, to defend our Serbian territory and our Orthodox religion. Thank you, Mr. President. "Radovan Karadzic: Cheers! "Zeljko Raznatovic: Very well, Mr. President. We are going back now. I want to thank you once again. "Radovan Karadzic: Good-bye! "Zeljko Raznatovic: Here we are, we will come and we will stay in contact."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, according to this document, is it footage that the Prosecution introduced into evidence? It says that it was filmed on the 10th of November, 1995. Now, what I'm interested in first is: Can you recognise the town, the town where this short film was taken?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the town and I recognise the footage. I'm just -- I'm just not sure of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the town is?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Bijeljina, and it's often shown on various footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, Karadzic says: "I thank you deeply and I congratulate you," among other things. Now, does that explain that Arkan came at Karadzic's invitation and that he stayed in Republika Srpska despite the position taken by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska right up until, as it says, November 1995, in the film?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said that I was a little taken aback by the date because we expelled Arkan, I believe, on the 9th of September. Now -- and that's the date of this document here too. So this official seeing-off, Karadzic could have done that on the 11th of September. Now, I see that you're mentioning the 11th of November here as the date. Now, in November there were intensive negotiations underway over Dayton and the peace agreement, Dayton Peace Agreement. So I think that the director of this footage took something -- some footage from an archive or he might have filmed it then. But anyway, with respect to these expressions of gratitude on the part of Karadzic, that's not a signal of any kind that Arkan came pursuant to his order. But the fact that Karadzic handed out these signs of recognition does show that Arkan came in with Karadzic's knowledge, which Karadzic at the time denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you can see that Arkan is addressing Karadzic in this film by using the words "supreme commander," right? He says "supreme commander" to him?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can see in this film is that they have -- neither of them have any knowledge of army discipline and touring the ranks, as you would normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, do you know who Milosav Gagovic is, Colonel Milosav Gagovic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Milosav Gagovic, a colonel, a Montenegrin, at the beginning of the war was assistant for the rear in the command of the 4th Corps in Sarajevo. Now, with the withdrawal of the JNA from Sarajevo, he stayed on for a time as the charge d'affaire or acting commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps until we established a full-fledged corps, or rather, the remains of the JNA 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So in May 1992, Colonel Gagovic performed this function, the one you've just described to us, if I understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he stayed on because in the Sarajevo barracks quite a number of cadets from the Yugoslav Army was blocked in the barracks and officers' families. So he stayed on until the end of May, until these people were pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, the Army of Republika Srpska, did it have -- establish military corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many there were and how they were organised? I know that it wasn't within your remit, but as a high-ranking officer I assume you have basic information about that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, at the beginning of the war there were four basic military courts: Banja Luka; Bijeljina; Sarajevo, or Sokolac, I'm not quite sure; and Bileca. And then sometime in the middle of the war the military court in Bileca, I think it was, was abolished and the basic military court in Sarajevo took over its affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any higher military courts or high military courts or anything like that? Supreme military court, did that exist?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a supreme military court, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, these military courts, were they in charge of dealing with crimes which the members of the Army of Republika Srpska committed, for example, against the civilian population or against prisoners of war to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that at a point in time all the trials of Serbs or members of the Army of Republika Srpska for crimes against other nations were stopped and that the trials and cases were activated only ten years later?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the trials were interrupted during the war. I can't remember exactly when that occurred, but I do know that they were reactivated -- I reactivated them as minister of defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they were interrupted?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the intervening years, did you perhaps learn who issued the order to stop the trials of crimes committed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that General Mladic did not. Now, who did, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honours, if I might confer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Petrovic, what you want to do with P59. You asked it to be shown on the screen, but do you want to have it admitted into evidence or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, according to my records this has already been admitted. If I'm mistaken, then I would like to tender it into evidence. But if I'm not mistaken, I think it has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it has been marked for identification. Is there any objection to admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the Prosecution originally tendered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, Stanisic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your position has changed since the 27th of August where you were objecting and wanted it to be MFI'd until completion of cross-examination of the witness through which it was tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, it has changed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has changed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- having listened to the cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then P59 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, earlier today by e-mail I notified the Chamber and Defence counsel of my intention to ask permission to re-open my direct examination to ask about an abbreviation found in the Mladic diary. I've been informed by both Defence teams that they do not oppose this request, so I'm asking the Court permission to ask a question with respect to that abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Permission is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, last week I showed you two diaries, and you recognised the handwriting of the author as General Ratko Mladic. We saw from your answers last week that General Mladic identified the speakers at meetings by their name or by their initials. My question to you is: How did General Mladic refer to you? I would ask that you simply tell us the convention that he used and provide us with a brief explanation, if possible. If a lengthy explanation is required, the Chamber might consider it prudent to do that in private session. Can you please briefly describe how General Mladic refers to you in his diaries?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NS, standing for the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on pages 4531 to 32 of the transcript, Mr. Jordash yesterday explored with you your first meeting with Mr. Stanisic, and in particular Badza's statement "I arrived here with my boss," and suggested to you that Badza was at that time the deputy minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia and in fact held a higher position than Stanisic. Did Jovica Stanisic during this meeting do anything which indicated to you that he considered Badza to be more senior than himself?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The two of them did not speak to each other, at least not at that meeting. There was no way for me to conclude who is whose boss or if indeed anybody was anybody else's boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you at any time during your stay at Mount Tara see Zoran Sokolovic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long all together were you present on Mount Tara at that time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1400 hours to 1700 hours, which means until dusk, I was in the helicopter. I had to return during day-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash suggested to you that Minister Sokolovic was in Bajina Basta that day. Are you able to tell us how far apart are Mount Tara and the town of Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how communication went between Hotel Mark and Bajina Basta, how far they were from each other, but as the crow flies it was about 20 kilometres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, yesterday Mr. Jordash asked you a number of questions related to Naser Oric and crimes perpetrated by him in the area of Skelani. I want to verify a passage with you. The record at page 4505, lines 13 and 14, records you as saying the following: "He," referring to Naser Oric, "he organised something that the Muslims called Patriotic League or the Red Berets that preceded the official establishment of the BiH Army." My question for you is the following: Is it your evidence that the members of the Patriotic League were also known as the Red Berets, or is that an error in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there is an error in the transcript. And there is another mistake in something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to give us the correction of this error, and then I'll ask you what the other error is that you've identified.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not wear red berets. I really don't know what was the context where you found this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you've just told us that you recall another error. Can you please tell us or describe what that error is.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remembered, but I simply concluded based on your question. Naser Oric did not establish either the Patriotic League or the Green Berets. The Patriotic League was established by the first commander of the so-called Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic. I probably meant, when it came to Oric, that the soldiers under his command were members of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. I was talking in general terms about Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were just one element or part of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday at pages 4512 to 4514 of the transcript, Mr. Jordash asked you a number of questions related to a video he identified as V000-2061 but did not show you. On page 4514 you attempted to describe what you recalled seeing on the tape. I want to now play you an excerpt that is approximately one minute long from that tape and ask you to verify is this the video that you and Mr. Jordash were discussing yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask Mr. Laugel at this time to play 65 ter 1561.1. It is an extract of a larger video. The clip that he will play is from one hour, 44 minutes, and 20 seconds, to one hour, 45 minutes, and 32 seconds in the original. The Prosecution does not seek to rely on what the speakers say, and it will be played without sound. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's only now that the French booth has finished its translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, since we are not listening to the audio here, can I ask you, is this the video that you were referring to in response to Mr. Jordash's questions?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I ask you to tell us the people that you recognise on this video?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see Nikola Sainovic on the screen at the moment. As for the other people surrounding him, I don't know any of them. And I also see the forehead belonging to Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders clip 1561.1 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just take brief instructions, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I inquire, first of all -- I'm not exactly sure what the Prosecution to show, so that would be my first query. If it's to show that Mr. Stanisic was present, there's no dispute about that. There is another concern, which is that the video earlier on that shows the minister present, Sokolovic, which is what we were discussing yesterday. So at the moment we object because it casts an impartial -- an incomplete picture, and we're not sure what the Prosecution want to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply want to clarify what was discussed yesterday. If -- I understand Mr. Jordash's point, he believes that maybe more of the video should be shown. I'm happy that the exhibit be marked for identification now and then whatever portion of this video Mr. Jordash wishes to have included in the excerpt, I'm happy to do that and report back to the Chamber next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think at this moment -- let me just check. One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm also prepared to agree, at this point, on the record, that Zoran Sokolovic is on the videotape earlier on and is present at this function, if that satisfies Mr. Jordash's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well the first purpose, from what I understand, is that where you referred to a video, Mr. Groome now plays it and says: Was this in your understanding the video you were asked about. So that has now been settled. The presence of Mr. Stanisic appears to be something there is no dispute about. Now, the third matter, would you be happy with, or does it add to your concern what Mr. Groome just stipulated?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, if it's the Prosecution's intent to identify for the Court what it was we were discussing yesterday in a clearer way and the Prosecution are happy to make that admission, then we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is what I wanted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's then clear. Then I hear of no objections from the Simatovic Defence. Mr. Registrar, the number of this video-clip which is played without sound would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P00398. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P398 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution at this time asks that 65 ter 1802 be placed on the screen for the witness to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, yesterday Mr. Jordash at pages 4490 to 4492 asked you questions about Red Berets in the Skelani area and what you knew about them. I would like you to take a look at 65 ter 1802, which is now appearing on the screen before you. Please read it. And when you are done so, please advise us whether you believe the document to be authentic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir. Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you able to tell -- there's several pages to this document. Perhaps if we could go to the last page, it has a stamp on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before we do that, I have an objection to the course the Prosecution wishes to take. And the objection is this, that I'm wondering if the General might be asked to remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would not be surprised if he understands or speaks English. Mr. Milovanovic, do you understand and speak English? Do you speak or understand any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, neither.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could you please take off your earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The objection is this, that the witness was indeed asked about Red Berets in the Skelani area at, Your Honours, page 4490 going into 4491. And I asked the witness whether he'd heard of a camp of Red Berets established and headed by Nikola Pupovac, one of Captain Dragan's pupils. And the witness answered: "I heard about that," looking at line 4, "I heard about that between the 16th and the 21st of January." So the witness confirmed that is what he'd heard about the Red Berets being headed by Nikola Pupovac. Now, my learned friend it seems is trying to contradict his own witness by putting in evidence that a group of Red Berets was, in fact, headed by Bozovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, is he, in this respect, his own witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You raised the matter, isn't it? You put these questions to him because you expected the witness to have knowledge which would be in support of your case, to the extent it was not an issue raised by the Prosecution. And therefore they're not turning against their own witness, but they are -- Mr. Groome is more or less cross-examining on what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- raised. And therefore, I do not fully understand your objection because it's different if you in re-examination -- than to -- well, more or less -- whether he's contradicting his own witness, as you said, or whether he is challenging what you elicited, which was new and not in the traditional cross-examination, that is, to challenge what the witness had said in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I would, with respect, stick to my objection, which is that the Prosecution ought not to be given an opportunity in re-examination to cross-examine their witness on issues they don't like. What they ought to do during re-examination is clarify issues for the Court, not simply say: Well, we don't like that piece of evidence, let's cross-examine the witness we called to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that mean that whatever you raised with the witness as not in response to what has been said, not challenging either substance or credibility or reliability of the witness or what he said in chief, that the Prosecution would have no opportunity to challenge the evidence which was then elicited newly in cross-examination under Rule 90(H)? That's a rather fundamental question I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, thinking about the jurisprudence, I think it's clearly something which different Trial Chambers do differently. In some Trial Chambers they would not permit re-examination to extend to

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Trial Chambers is that almost always re-examination is limited to clarifying issues which have arisen during cross-examination, but not seeking during that process to controvert one's own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't understand how I'm trying to controvert my own witness. Over two pages of transcript were devoted to the Red Berets and what was their organisational structure in Skelani. I didn't lead that evidence. I believe there's confusion around that issue now, and there's a report by the Army of Republika Srpska that spells out what they knew about these Red Berets in the Skelani area in May of 1993. I'm just seeking to clarify that point, and I think the easiest way to do it is to simply have the witness verify the authenticity of the document and introduce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me confer with my colleagues first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber's ruling is that the objection is denied. The matter on which the -- Mr. Groome now examines the witness was brought up by the Defence and was not in response to a matter which was raised in the examination-in-chief; and under those circumstances, the Chamber considers it fair that Mr. Groome further examines the witness. Therefore, you may proceed. But we'd invite -- Mr. Milovanovic, could you put on your earphones again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to the last page in that document.

utterances.speaker: THE TENDERING PARTY
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, I've asked that the last page of the document be shown to you. There is an endorsement or a stamp on that last page, and ask you to look at that endorsement and see whether you are now able to make an assessment as to whether this document is an authentic one?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE TENDERING PARTY
utterances.text: And does this document provide a contemporaneous report about what was known about the Red Beret unit in Skelani during the period covered by the report?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me or could you please return the heading of this document. I am interested in the date. The date will allow me to answer your question. Very well. I believe that this document is indeed authentic.

utterances.speaker: THE TENDERING PARTY
utterances.text: And is it a contemporaneous report about what was known about the Red Beret unit in Skelani during this period?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is an interim report sent by the commander of the Skelani Battalion to the commander of the Drina Corps at their special request. This does not belong to the group of regular combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender 65 ter 1802 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P00399. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P399 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE TENDERING PARTY
utterances.text: Now, General, near the end of the hearings yesterday Mr. Jordash asked you a number of questions related to Operation Pauk. During the course of these questions you referred at page 4540, line 12 of the transcript to being tricked into attending a meeting held on the 8th of November, 1994, in Slunj and attended by 11 officers and Fikret Abdic and Jovica Stanisic. Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I said 11 officers of Fikret Abdic, meaning 11 Muslim officers, amongst others.

utterances.speaker: THE TENDERING PARTY
utterances.text: Now, so that the record is clear, this is a different meeting than the one you described last week held in Petrova Gora in February 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meeting preceded the meeting in Petrova Gora. The difference between the two was about four months.

utterances.speaker: THE TENDERING PARTY
utterances.text: So you met with Jovica Stanisic on two occasions in relation to Operation Pauk; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. On the first occasion we didn't speak, we both listened to the others; and on the second occasion, we did speak.

utterances.speaker: THE TENDERING PARTY
utterances.text: Now, in your discussion with Mr. Jordash about this November 1994 meeting, you said something I want to clarify. At page 4542 of the transcript on lines 1 to 4 you said the following: "The Serb army of the Krajina wanted to resuscitate Fikret Abdic's army, and for that purpose I was supposed to give them 6.000 barrels and Celeketic would give them 5.000 and that I was supposed to launch an offensive towards Bihac with my forces." Can you clarify what you were referring to when you said 6.000 barrels and 5.000 barrels?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant rifles.

utterances.speaker: THE TENDERING PARTY
utterances.text: Now, my last question to you here today is: Mr. Petrovic asked you to characterise the Pauk operation and you did so at page 27, line 1, of today's transcript as follows: "It was a temporary force to carry out a certain task." My question to you is the following: Do you know whether Novakovic's authority over non-VRS personnel during Operation Pauk was temporary in nature or -- temporary in nature for that specific operation or was of some more permanent nature?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a bit more permanent. If you were following my testimony today, there was a document in front of me that was my order to the command of the 2nd Corps and the 1st Corps. And the order was to resubordinate one corps --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the numbers of units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for those to be resubordinated to General Novakovic. And from that moment until the end of the mission, General Novakovic was in command of those units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, could you please repeat the numbers that were part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE TENDERING PARTY
utterances.text: General, the interpreters didn't understand the numbers that you referred to. I think you were referring to or you were identifying different corps.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the signal to be able to start to speak. Okay. Now I have it. The following were resubordinated to the Pauk Operative Group: One battalion from the 16th Motorised Brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps and one battalion from the 11th Krupa Brigade of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE TENDERING PARTY
utterances.text: My follow-up question then is: If members of those non-VRS units were transferred away from the area before the completion of Pauk, would General Novakovic have retained operational control over those non-VRS personnel?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those battalions were resubordinated to him only for that particular mission, and the mission was to break-up the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no questions. Mr. Jordash, if you have any questions which were triggered by the re-examination, please proceed. Let's keep an eye on the clock. How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's a very discreet issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because we have to deal with scheduling issues as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be extremely brief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I refer you back to the report we have just looked at, Mr. Milovanovic, P399. And you make the point that from your expertise it's an interim report which did not belong to the group of regular combat reports. What's the significance of it being an interim report rather than a regular combat report?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An interim report is sent when something needs to be specially explained about what's happening at the front, that kind of thing. And I said - and I stand by that - that the Drina Corps command asked for a report about the behaviour and conduct of the Red Berets from the local commander. Now, whether anybody asked the Drina Corps, the Army of Republika Srpska, that is not something we can see from this document. But we do see that the commander of the Drina Corps requested information about the conduct of the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would there normally be a follow-up report on such an interim report?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. No further questions by the Simatovic Defence. Mr. Milovanovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for -- not only for coming but having to wait for quite a while in The Hague and having received homework to be done. I would like to thank you very much for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. I am just addressing the parties for one second. In view of the new material that has arrived and which would not exclude for the possibility that further questions may be put to this witness in relation to that material as well, that it is so uncertain that I would not give any specific instructions about contacts the witness may have. Mr. Groome, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution would agree with that approach, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the Defence as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We agree with that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, I'll refrain from giving any further instructions. Mr. Milovanovic, I had to raise this small procedural issue which remains without any consequences. Finally, I was informed that there's a fair chance that you'll get a flight tomorrow so that you are home again as soon as possible. You are excused. Could you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the last matter I'd like to raise is the agreement which was reached between the parties as to the next witness to be called. The Chamber understands that the parties would agree to the following, that is, that Witness JF-049 would be rescheduled to the week of the 17th of May, provided that there could be a third day of proceedings to be added to the schedule of that week and also the week after that, the 24th of May. Further, the Prosecution will redact, although from what I see, a limited portion of the new 92 ter statement. The Stanisic and Simatovic Defence would then agree to sit a third day during that week. Mr. Stanisic, I hope you were consulted on that, but there is a fair chance that we would then sit three days the week of the 17th and the week of the 24th of May and that under those circumstances the opposition to the admission of the 8th of April, 2010, statement of Witness JF-049 would be withdrawn. And the same would be true for the associated exhibits related to that 92 ter statement. Now as a -- finally then Witness JF-032 would then be called to give testimony next week. Now, from what I've seen, Witness 32 is -- there's quite a lot of material, 92 ter material, presented in relation to that witness. Also, I do understand that the substance of the testimony, there are no [sic] protective measures for that from what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just check, but I believe there are protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are -- I didn't say that there are no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was voice distortion, face distortion, pseudonym, but not private or closed session, although portions of the evidence may be given in private or closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That witness has been scheduled for two hours examination-in-chief. We have two days available next week. Could the Defence teams, who apparently -- are aware of Witness D -- 32 to replace Witness JF-049. How much time would they need for cross-examination of this witness as far as matters stand now? Could we conclude the testimony of that witness if the Prosecution takes two hours within those two days?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I'm fairly confident we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we'll be able to complete the cross-examination within two days as well. And if I might add, I am fully conscious that my English is far from perfect but I think that we did manage to reach an agreement with our learned friends of the Prosecution that one day next week will be given to 042, Witness 042, and not in two weeks -- or did I understand it wrongly? It says here that we're going to have the week beginning of the 17th and the week beginning of the 24th, to have them in both weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at least what appears in an e-mail that was forwarded to the Chamber and which originates from Mr. Weber and is addressed to Mr. Knoops and Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, so the agreement as I understand it is that we would proceed with 32. We would not begin 49's testimony until the week of the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the -- yes. A third day would be provided, then, for the week of the 17th and also for the week of the 24th. I don't know for what purpose exactly but that apparently is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still for --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's to avoid having to reschedule all the 10 witnesses that would follow. So we would appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's a request rather than a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To plug JF-049 in the existing schedule rather than move all the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's then clear. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: If possible - we understand the problems of the Prosecution - but if possible if the Prosecution could look for just this day in the week of the 17th of May and not the 24th, if that's possible, because of the -- also condition of Mr. Stanisic. That's our request, to take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think it was for both weeks, so not for the one week or the other, but for both weeks a third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's our estimate that JF-049 would take two days, and that's why I was suggesting two days. But I can work out those details with Mr. Knoops next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, finally, I have to -- of course, most of the Judges sitting in this case -- all of the Judges sitting in this case have other cases ongoing. We have a fair expectation that we could sit for a third day in those weeks, and we commit ourselves to do our utmost best to make that possible. But some decisions still have to be taken in other cases which we do not expect to influence our expectation that we could sit three days during the week of the 17th and the 24th, but we cannot exclude that for the full hundred per cent. But our commitment is fully there and our expectations are high. Any other matter? I'm not encouraging you to do it because my bad reputation will be reconfirmed, that is, to go beyond the scheduled time. If not, we adjourn. And we'll resume on Monday, the 3rd of May, quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom II.
